stem:
An old-age psychiatrist reviews a 74-year-old three months after effective treatment of a first depressive episode. Mood, sleep, appetite and motivation have returned to baseline, and he again enjoys company. His daughter still has to supervise bills and medicines because of repeated errors; the difficulties have progressed despite the mood improvement. Physical examination, medication review and initial blood tests have not identified another reversible cause.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrange comprehensive cognitive and functional assessment
options.explanation: Persistent, progressive functional impairment after mood improvement warrants further assessment for a coexisting neurocognitive disorder. A depressive episode does not settle the cause of every cognitive symptom.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase antidepressant treatment for residual cognitive symptoms
options.explanation: The mood syndrome has responded, while the cognitive problem has not. Increasing medication without reassessing the formulation may add adverse effects and delay the appropriate investigation.

options.label: C
options.text: Attribute the ongoing cognitive impairment to the depressive episode
options.explanation: Cognitive impairment may improve with depression treatment, but recovery is not guaranteed and conditions can coexist. Reassurance alone would ignore the observed functional decline.

options.label: D
options.text: Start donepezil for presumed Alzheimer disease
options.explanation: The history does not yet establish a dementia subtype or an indication for donepezil. Assessment should precede disease-specific prescribing.

options.label: E
options.text: Continue mood treatment and repeat cognition in six months
options.explanation: Continue appropriate mood care, but do not postpone assessment of the progressive cognitive and functional errors for another six months. Recovery of mood has not resolved these problems.

context: Mood recovery and cognitive recovery are separate outcomes; persistent functional decline needs its own assessment.
